utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, it is case, IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor against Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to greet everybody as usual, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and all the personnel that is supporting the work of this courtroom. I have four oral decisions to render but before that I give the floor to the registrar to give us IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] Following parties have tendered lists of exhibits tendered through the witness Ismet Poljarevic. The list tend tendered by the OTP will be given IC number 179. The list of exhibits tendered through 2D will be given Exhibit number IC 180. The list by 4D will be given Exhibit number IC 181. And the list by 6D will be given exhibit number IC 182. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Oral decision number 1, regarding exhibits introduced through Witness CK, who was heard on the 4th of December 2006. The Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits presented by the Prosecution as they have certain probative value and certain relevance. P 09799 under seal. As regards Exhibits P 03160 and P 09086, put forward by the Prosecution, the Chamber notes that these were already admitted on the 11th and 13th December 2006 respectively. In addition, the Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits tendered by the Praljak Defence as they have certain probative value and certain relevance. P 03214 and P 03991. Oral decision number 2, regarding exhibits introduced through Witness CM, who appeared before the Court on the 5th of December 2006. The Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits tendered by the Prosecution through lists IC 00157, and IC 00171, as they have certain probative value and certain relevance. It is note worthy that Exhibits P 09753 and IC 00137 referred to in these lists are admitted under seal. Also, the Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits tendered by the Stojic Defence and mentioned in list IC 00163 as it has certain probative value and certain relevance. Oral decision number 3, concerning exhibits introduced through the testimony of Witness CN, who was heard on the 6th of December 2006. The Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits tendered by the Prosecution as they have certain probative value and relevance: P 09754 under seal, P 01900, P 09285. The Chamber would like to remind you that Exhibits P 09086 and P 03057 were admitted on the 13th and 14th December 2006 respectively. Oral decision number 4, the last one, concerning exhibits, in this case exhibits introduced through Witness CP who was heard on the 7th December 2006. The Trial Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits tendered by the Prosecution as they have certain probative value and certain relevance: P 09755, under seal; P 09104; IC 00115. I would now like to ask the registrar to move us into private session. For a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that the Prosecution needs 20, 25 more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I'm aiming for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are resuming our hearing and I will now give the floor to Mr. Kruger who will continue his examination, his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon or yesterday evening, when we broke, you had told the Court about an incident where you said Mujo Zuhric had been rounded up and taken off and he never returned. If we can look at that incident for a moment, when you say he was rounded up and taken off, was that from the hangar where you were being held in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from hangar number 3. He sat three or four metres in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And under what circumstances was he taken away?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard later that they were taking him home, they had taken him home, to fetch some money. I think that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who had taken him away?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, only military police had access to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And once again, these military police, from which organisation were they?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, did you at any stage later find out what had happened to Mujo Zuhric?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. His body was found and was later buried. It was established that he was murdered, an autopsy was per formed. Everything was done. At any rate, he was buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When was his body found?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly, but it happened when it was finally possible to search that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was anybody else taken away from your hangar during that period you were in it?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Another younger man was taken away. His name was Zujo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court the circumstances under which Zujo was taken away?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He used to sit to my right, about seven metres away from me, close to the wall, and one guard whom we called Shorty, some people knew him personally, insisted that we enlarge those corridors, as we called them, to squeeze together a little more so that they would be more comfortable passing through, and this Zujo, I don't know what came over him, told the guard, "You mean the corridor to Neum or until Neum." I don't know why he said that but we had learned in those days that there were some negotiations going on and he made that remark, that allusion, something to the effect that Alija wants to go to Neum that's probably why he was taken away. This Shorty, called Nikola Andrun, who was on duty then, he was on duty as deputy warden of the camp and Zujo was taken away, never to be seen again. I really don't know what happened to him. Of course, I know that later he was found. An autopsy was performed and he was buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You've already mentioned a few of the personnel at the camp, Shorty, Marko, Nikola Andrun, Bosko Previsic, could you tell the court from your experience in Gabela, who were the personnel manning this detention centre?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without a doubt, Bosko Previsic. He was the be all and end all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And who were the people under him or from what organisation were they, if you know? Or unit?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to qualify it, but all the services that were active there and all the guards, everything was under his command, everything and everyone was subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The guards who were working there, were they older people or regular soldiers or regular military policemen?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the composition was heterogenous. There were younger people and not so young, middle aged men, even some on the other side of 40, maybe my age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The guards who were working there, did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were all in uniforms, and armed, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you have any idea from which region any of these guards came from or their units?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that some were locals, some were from Konjic. I know one man in particular who was particularly vile. He was from Konjic and that's even what we called him, the Konjic man. And he also had another nickname and the nickname was "is that fair?" Whenever he played some nasty trick on somebody or did something evil to someone he would say, "Now, isn't that fair?" And this Konjic man had a favourite thing, and that was to make people lie down on the concrete and pretend they are swimming. That was really humiliating and awful sight to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just on this point, you have also mentioned Marko. Did Marko have any peculiarity or any habit in this regard, in making the prisoners do anything?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Marko was the first person I got to know in Gabela. He met us at the gate. He interrogated us when we came. But already that first evening, or, rather, first night after midnight, he came to the hangar, yelling, of course, he made us lie down and stick our noses into the concrete and kept us lying like that for a long time, I don't know for how long. But I know that my back was hurting awfully and it seemed it would break. He said he would shoot if anybody dared raise their head, and he even fired a shot, although not at us but at the wall. One thing that sticks in my mind in particular from that night is this: There was a man together with us from Stolac, Smajo he was a big man, bulky, but he had advanced diabetes. He was already at the end of his tether when he was brought in, but still he found the strength, he found it in him to ask that man for more water. He was probably having a crisis. However, Marko hit him with a rifle butt or with his rifle. Any way, I couldn't see properly, but we could recognise the sound and we later did see that he had hit Smajo. We thought he wouldn't survive but he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you mentioned that persons, both military and then civilians, came from outside the camp during the first period you were held there, shall I say detention centre, and that they abused detainees. Did this practice stop at any stage?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those raids were more frequent and more brutal at the beginning, those assaults against inmates were more frequent and more violent. However, as of the 13th, it already began on the 13th, I'm sorry I lost the thread. Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. What I would like to know is, when you arrived from the 17th onwards, you mentioned during that period that people from outside the camp had come in, you mentioned specifically the big military policeman and then the athletically built civilian at one stage?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did that practice stop at any stage?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes, it did stop. To our great joy and satisfaction, although the violence, the practice of removing people and killing them did not stop. From a certain moment on, only the military police of the HVO had access to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the date but I know that it was several days after I was detained. The commander, Bosko Previsic brought something on a piece of paper, he read it out standing in the door, and he stuck the paper to the wall, or to the door, I don't remember, but I understood the point of that text. It said that he was prohibiting entry to groups and individuals. The gist of it was that only the military police had authorised access.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did that in actual fact occur after that, that only military police had access to people with -- or detainees within the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, in fact, occur. From that moment on, only the military policemen came in, they would sometimes remove people, sometimes those people wouldn't come back. We later heard that some of those people had been killed. However, we were relieved to some extent and we were less anxious for our safety. At least we knew that it was only them, that it was no longer the case that any outsider could come in as they pleased and attack us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What about the camp personnel? Did any further mistreatment at their hands occur?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you about the personnel among the guards, this man from Konjic was especially bad. He mistreated us enough for all of them. I think he was a sadist. He had the need to abuse people. He would take people out, beat them up, mistreat them, brutalise them, but on the other hand, there were guards who were very correct, decent, who were human, and as for some of them you could see that they found it hard to be there at all, that they had to be there because they were mobilised or for some other reason and it was obvious that they were not getting any pleasure from their position there. And that gave me some reassurance that there were human beings around us after all, that we would survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have just broached a subject that I wanted to question you on. You have already answered some of my questions, in fact. You said that among guards, there were those who did not share the attitude and approach of their other colleagues. They had orders that they had to carry out. What I want to know is this: Since you were there on the spot, you were a victim, the conduct that you have described in your eyes, was it dictated by individual character, such as that of this sadist that you mentioned, or was it dictated by instructions or orders such as from the camp commander, which resulted in this particular outcome? Have you thought about this? And as somebody who was an eyewitness, what do you think about this conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that it was up to the individuals. One person would behave in one way, another person behaved in another way, and I don't actually think that anybody ordered anything or maybe they misinterpreted an order, perhaps, where they were told to be a little stricter so I don't know what this tolerance level was but I don't think anybody, how could a normal person order anything like that? I think it depended on the personality of the person concerned, their mental makeup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, do you think that the director of the camp was aware of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am certain that he knew about it, and he opted to gloss over it, but on the other hand, I don't think he ordered individuals to behave the way they did. I have no reason to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's a precise answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you had contacts with the guards, when you came into contact with the guards, were there any oral exchanges with the guards or were you forbidden to speak to them? And that you weren't able to say anything to them because this was not authorised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's difficult for me now to explain that and answer it but I think I follow your question. There was a strict regime by which we weren't allowed to move around. It wasn't forbidden for us to talk to guards. I don't know whether the guards were forbidden to talk to us but I do know that people did talk to them. For example, the same day when one of my colleagues was beaten up, an inmate, that same day a guard talked to me, we had a conversation, a very frank one. So I understood this as the guard being sorry for what had happened and that he was sorry for the man who had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Now, you said that you had a conversation with a guard concerning this particular event. When you had conversations of that kind, private conversations with the guard, would the guard be conscious of the fact that in future, inevitably, everything would come out one day or another, and people would be held accountable? Did the guard realise that? Was he aware of what could come to pass in the future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. I can't say, Your Honour, what the guard thought. Sometimes I thought he had had a drink. But he was very lucid in his thinking and showed a humane character and even addressed me as "Efendi," so he knew that I was what I was, that I had that post, and so the conversation relaxed me. And had it not been for that violence to my colleague, whom they beat up, I would have considered that and remembered that as one of the better days in camp, the conversation with that guard meant a great deal to me, because it was important that you could see that there were human beings and this was a human being that I had in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, my last question but there is another question from the Bench, my last question is as follows: You are a cultivated, well-educated man. When you were confronted with these guards, from your point of view, what was their intellectual level? High? Medium? Average? Zero? What would you say? Could you gauge the character and intellectual capacity of the guards, whether they had a full awareness of the events they were involved in and mixed up in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the makeup was heterogenous. There were different people. I don't think among the guards that any of them had a university education or training but regardless of their level of education, they were able to think clearly. So some people thought one way. They acted in different ways and thought in different ways. I don't think it's always important whether you're educated or not, that this doesn't -- your behaviour doesn't necessarily depend on that but I don't think there were any university-educated guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Witness, if I understood you correctly, you said that the camp commander certainly knew about what was going on and your suffering, but that you weren't sure that he had received instructions to mistreat you. That's the first point. And the second point, the second thing you said is that you were able to speak to your guards, and have exchanges with them, conversations with them. Now, my question is this: Was it possible for you to send out a message about your suffering and explain the maltreatment you were subjected to, to the authorities, to the commander of the prison, through one channel or another and to send the message out to a superior authority? If you didn't do this yourself, do you know whether anybody else did? Whether the authorities were aware, the superior authorities, superior to the prison commander, whether they were aware of your suffering? Could you get a message through to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that was impossible. It was impossible to send out information like that, because the commander of the prison was himself very brutal. He beat people up. So he was in that, and we couldn't complain to him, certainly not, and as to a higher authority, we couldn't do that either, certainly not. We weren't in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, did you witness the visit of a military officer, a brigadier Dzanko to Gabela?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you give the Court an idea of when this was in relation to when you arrived at the camp or at the detention facility, centre?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it took place some 10 days after my arrival there, after I was brought there, 10 days probably later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what happened exactly when Brigadier Dzanko came?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all we heard a heated discussion in front of the hangar. We didn't know about the visit. Nobody informed us of it. So we thought it was a spontaneous visit but anyway we did hear this conversation, and realised that it was Bosko Previsic talking to someone, but we didn't know who the other person was, who the visitor was. However, they had a short conversation outside. It was a heated conversation, a heated exchange, and then they went in through the door, the door that I was by, the first door into the hangar, and the man introduced himself. We wondered and tried to guess who he could be, but he said quite openly and introducing himself he said, "I am Brigadier Dzanko." I think that's what he said, brigadier Dzanko, an officer of the Croatian army, and he said that he was there on a private visit and that he had some former soldiers, as I understood it - I think that's what he said - who were with him fighting on the southern battle front. But any way he said he'd come on a private visit so that was that. He toured the hangar, went around the compound, got to see the entire hangar, how the people lived, what their living conditions were like, and he could see that there were no adequate living conditions at all. I think he spoke to some of the inmates for brief moments but any way he insisted straight away, he said that the windows should be opened straight away, and there was a line of windows, small windows, right at the top under the roof, and they were hermetically sealed. He said that the windows should be opened because the door was closed and the windows were closed and we had no air at all. And Boko said or rather not Boko but the commander, Bosko Previsic said that it was impossible to open the windows, that they didn't open, or rather it was impossible because they were very high up. And the other man said, "Well, bring in some ladders or whatever and I'll open the windows myself." Boko said, "We'll do that later, we'll open them later on," but of course he didn't. So that's more or less what happened. That was what the visit was like. We thought the visit was good for us. We felt a certain amount of change. That is to say, the doors were open more frequently, we were given a little more water to drink, little things like that. So the visit was useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you hear any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I, perhaps I'm anticipating on you but it strikes me, Witness, that in your written statement, you have said that after that visit, the windows were in fact opened. Now you have said that it never happened. I see a certain contradiction there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think the windows were opened. Perhaps the doors were opened more frequently. But I don't exclude the possibility that I might have forgotten what actually happened but I don't think now thinking about it that the windows were actually ever opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you're note sure, is that a correct summing up of your actual situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd rather venture to say that the windows weren't opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear any other conversation between Boko Previsic and Brigadier Dzanko on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a conversation, a dialogue, in front of the hangar, when they arrived. Well, roughly speaking, what I heard was the substance, the gist of it, and that was, well, he cautioned him, he warned him, and said, more or less, it's not your fault or perhaps it's not your fault, I don't know what he used, that the people are here but you will certainly be responsible for the way in which they live, for the conditions in which they are living, for the fact that they have no air to breathe and no water to drink. Roughly along those lines. He issued a caution. He warned him in that kind of way. That's how I understood it and that's what I actually heard him say more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who cautioned who or who said that to whom?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigadier Dzanko said that to Boko, to the commander of the camp. .

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: With the assistance of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Witness, please, Brigadier Dzanko who apparently belonged to the Croatian army on the basis of what you told us. Perhaps I missed that part, but was he wearing civilian clothes or uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was wearing a uniform. He was in military gear. He looked like a real officer. He looked very dignified and acted in a dignified manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were there any insignia on his uniform, any decorations, patches, flashes, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really couldn't say. Since he introduced himself, it didn't seem important. He didn't have any weapons. He had a broad military belt, army belt. I remember that, green. I can't say whether he actually had any insignia or stripes or decorations or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, since you saw him and heard what he said and you were an audio witness, you heard their conversation, how could you explain the presence of an officer, a foreign general, on the soil of your own country? Did you ever wonder why or did it seem quite normal to you or did you ask yourself any questions about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as Brigadier Dzanko is concerned, all of us saw him. He toured the compound, the whole hangar and everybody saw him. And everybody, I think, could hear him too although I was perhaps in the best position to hear him because I was close by the door. At that particular moment, it wasn't important to me, I didn't think about things like that actually. The most important thing was for the conditions to be improved a little bit so that we could have better conditions there, at least a little better. Now, whether he was Croatian, from Croatia, well you couldn't really differentiate what was what but everything was Croatian at the time, the soil, the air, everything was Croatian there. So I didn't have to think much about that, and to be quite honest, I didn't give it much thought at the time. Of course, I knew what it meant, from the aspects of the sovereignty of the country I belonged to, that is to say Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that's another story again. At the time, that visit meant to me, or rather it was the priority demand to have living conditions improve and not to think about anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You gave us a detail a moment ago in saying that this Croatian general was paying the visit, paying a private visit, and you even added that there were in Gabela soldiers whom he had commanded previously. Now, these soldiers, were they HVO soldiers or were they soldiers, Muslim soldiers, who were incarcerated, who were imprisoned there? Which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think or rather I don't think, I'm quite sure, that they were Bosniaks, Muslims, who were in the HVO previously, in the previous period, and I assume, and I do believe, that they fought together with him, that they were engaged in combat with him. They were in his unit. He was their commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you correctly, former Muslim soldiers who had fought with Brigadier Dzanko found themselves at that point in time prisoners in Gabela, these former soldiers belonging to this brigadier's unit. Were they able to meet the brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't know. He did speak to a few people. Now, whether he knew those people he approached and talked to I really can't say. I don't know. But the fact is that a whole two HVO brigades were manned exclusively with Bosniaks. They were exclusively Bosniak units with a commander who was a Bosniak and the people were rounded up, arrested, and sent to Dretelj camp and some to Gabela, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I can refer the witness to Exhibit 3731, if we could perhaps call that up on the e-court, although with the assistance of the usher the witness could perhaps just look at the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document and its attachment is a report from, or purports to be a report from Nedjeljko Obradovic to General Petkovic, and attached to it is a statement by Bosko Previsic, which purports to be signed by Bosko Previsic. They are both handwritten. Is it correct that the day before yesterday, you saw this document when I showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In your mind, what is reported in this document, does it refer to the incident that you've just described to the Chamber about the visit of Brigadier Dzanko?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date coincides, and it's roughly what he said, some 10 days after I was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise to Mr. Kruger for intervening but it would be a good idea to draw your attention to the fact that the date is wrong in the English version. It says August in the English, whereas in the B/C/S it says July, the 27th of July. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, Your Honour, to be quite precise, in the heading of the document and in the text of the document, the translation is quite wrong, as to the month, because in B/C/S, the month throughout is July, whereas the English translation has August throughout. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I thank my learned colleagues for pointing that out to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, the one thing that I would just wish to draw your attention to before moving on is, in the attachment, and that would be on the next page, that is the handwritten statement purported to be by Boko Previsic, towards or in the final paragraph on that page, it states -- he states, "That is the situation now, that he thought it would get better. 'It is good here,' he said. As far as he could see it was not as terrible as he had been told." Now this refers to or this is Boko Previsic's version of what Brigadier Dzanko said. To your recollection, from what you heard, is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of this statement by the commander Boko Previsic. I don't think it's correct except when he mentioned Dzanko, the brigadier. About all the rest, Brigadier Dzanko never said any of that. Dzanko didn't say any of this. He didn't say this. He was visibly upset by what he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say he was visibly upset, from -- what did you observe that makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his reaction, the way he reacted, what he demanded of Boko, the commander, Bosko Previsic, his facial expression while he was saying it. I think that I assessed this state of mind of his very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, before finalising on Gabela, I would like to show you one picture and that is Exhibit 9016 and it was page 12 of the set of photographs. There are two photographs on that page. The usher will assist you in a moment or will call it up on the screen. No. It's not that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps if we could put it on the ELMO, it will be very brief. I've just heard it was page 16, sorry. I had it marked wrong in my version. There it is. That's the one which is now called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, this hangar, this is a picture of a hangar in Gabela. My simple question is: Is this similar to the hangar that you were held in, hangar number 3?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what hangar number 3 was like, the one I was in. Two wide doors, a platform for unloading and loading of trucks, roughly that's what it looked like, yes. And the other two hangars looked like that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you look at the side wall, there are some windows which can be seen just behind the trees. Did your hangar also have such little windows?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were little windows like that, right underneath the roof, high up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we could move down and look at the second picture on that page, and that is the back view of such a hangar. Did your hangar have similar windows to those depicted in this picture?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just such windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, is it correct that on the 24th of September 1993, you were released from Gabela?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And that's the date on the piece of paper releasing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Had you been warned previously that you would have been released or not?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know in advance. I didn't even know that day, although it was in the air that something was going on and I had an inkling that maybe we would be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Boko Previsic himself drove you to Capljina, where you were placed in a house with a number of other imams who had been released from Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, could you name some of those imams who were there with you in that location?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sakib Kadric and his son, Omer. I think he was a student in his second year. Sakib Kovacic [phoen]. Ibrahim Blazevic, Ahmed Alic, and Numan Cosic. Those were mainly imams from the neighbouring parishes or dzemats, as we called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in this location in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of days, three or four days maybe, until the 29th, when we were moved to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And how did it come that you were moved to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the only way we could go. They wouldn't let us go to Bosnia, although we wanted to go there, because our families were in Bosnia, everybody's families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who wouldn't allow you to go to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say "they wouldn't let us go to Bosnia," who were you referring to? Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO, the HVO wouldn't let us. The authorities and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you require any authorisation to go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to get that. Otherwise we wouldn't have been able to cross the border and leave Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What kind of authorisation was this?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that during those few days that I was in Capljina, we actually did get a paper from Zagreb containing some sort of guarantee for our stay in Croatia. I think somebody had to assume responsibility for us. And that paper bore the signature of Dr. Adalbert Rebic. I think he was head of the refugee office, and the mufti, Sevko Omerbasic, who was the main imam there in Zagreb, and after that came, we got our papers allowing us to leave Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From Croatia, where did you go to from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed for two months in Croatia, some went on to Germany, before two months were out, to join their families. And I stayed for two months in Podgora.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And after two months in Podgora, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1993, I went to Germany and I stayed there until the end of June next year when I returned to Sarajevo and then to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did you rejoin your wife and children in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had already returned to Sarajevo after all the suffering they had been through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want to touch upon one final aspect with you. You have mentioned that you -- or you've testified about seeing the mosques in Recice, Lokve and Aladinici burning. As an imam in that region, did you then or subsequently find out about the destruction of any other mosques in your religious community or the general area of your religious community?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I only had an opportunity to see the mosque in Visici. As we were leaving Capljina on the way to Croatia, I could see that nothing remained of the mosque. There was not a single stone left standing. Everything had been blown up and completely removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, a final question, then. To your knowledge, as an imam, what was the purpose, to your mind, for the destruction of these mosques that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I know the reason, I'm pretty sure. The reason was to destroy and remove all the traces of Islamic tradition and culture, anything that could remind people of Muslims, so that they would never come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you, as a Bosniak, and the people from your community who were removed from that area, what would that mean or how would that affect your ability to return to that area subsequently?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, it made their return more difficult because even when people started to return, it was made more difficult in those areas where religious buildings had been destroyed - plus there were threats and intimidation - and the first thing people did was to clean up their cemeteries, rebuild mosques, and only after that, rebuild their own houses. That's how return started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And from what period did that return start? And that's my final question.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to tell you when that was because I was already in Mostar in July 1994, I was already involved in my work as imam, I had my duties, and job, and I couldn't really go. I had already tried to go to Visici together with some people, two busloads of people, to see the cemetery there, and Mufti Smajkic was with me but we only managed to go to Buna. We were stopped there by the police, with dogs, and we had to turn back, so we didn't succeed that time. Later on, they started burying the bodies. People started returning, humanitarian organisations helped to rebuild houses, and even mosques were rebuilt and renewed. I am rather happy, in fact, with the situation now. It has improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. The Prosecution has no further questions at this stage. The remaining documents in the bundle, the Prosecution will submit at a different stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's best to take our break now, and we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before I give the floor to the Defence who will have two and a half hours, there is a question that I wanted to ask and didn't. This commander, Bosko Perisic, do you know whether subsequently, in the years that followed, was he ever prosecuted in your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I know that he was tried in Mostar and I think he escaped. He is now a fugitive from justice. He left Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You say that there was a trial, but to your knowledge, he's a fugitive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the Prosecution will have some more information to give us later. Mr. Mundis, do you have any information about this person?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we are taking certain steps to obtain this type of information. I'm not in a position right now to answer that question with any degree of certainty. But we -- I assure you based on the Trial Chamber's earlier comments regarding some of the cases ongoing in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that we are taking steps to obtain this type of information and perhaps sometime in the early part of next year we might be in a position to have more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to clarify the situation because my client said, and the witness also said, that the gentleman is a fugitive from justice. There are proceedings ongoing against him but what I want to say is that a verdict has been pronounced just today about -- against his deputy, before the Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we'll learn about that later. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours. We have no questions for the gentleman and wish to thank him for coming and giving his evidence. General Praljak has asked for our time. We have provided it to the general, with the proviso that he use it wisely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid all problems with time, two hours and a half, that's 150 minutes divided by six, that's 27 minutes each. Ms. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start my examination, I wish to inform you that I received ten minutes from the Coric Defence and ten minutes from the Pusic Defence, but I will use that additional time only if I really need it. Maybe I'll be able to complete within my own time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kajmovic.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have just a few questions for you, and they relate only to your humanitarian work. We highly appreciate, all of us in the Defence team, the testimony that you gave and since we do not often get witnesses from non-governmental humanitarian organisations, we want to clarify just a few points and go through a few documents that have to do precisely with Merhamet. I have to warn you that we must make a brief pause between questions and answers because we speak the same language and we must allow the interpreters to do their work for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and the others. Is it correct that at that time, in 1992 and 1993 that you testified about, when you worked in Merhamet, Merhamet's main logistical bases were in Split and Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have already said that for the most part, both we and Caritas got supplies from the UNHCR, and that was supplemented by what we got from Split and Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We are not going to deal with the UNHCR. I would like to concentrate on Merhamet and I know that Merhamet performed one part of the job in supplying the civilians with basic necessities, whereas the greatest part of this work was done by the UNHCR. Speaking about Croatia, many organisations were set up at that time in Croatia to send aid to Bosnia and Herzegovina, 228 in total is the figure I have, and 119 were actually from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that I never went to Zagreb in my line of work. I went to Split several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is it the case that the Islamic community and Merhamet, together with the SDA in mid-1992 and 1993 were involved in certain issues that were important to the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The times were very tempest two us and hardly anyone could remain standing by but I don't think I noticed any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I think that something got lost in interpretation or the record, when my colleague asked the last question, whether the witness had knowledge about the activity of various humanitarian organisations in Croatia. The second part of the answer was recorded and the first part was when the witness said, "Yes, I do have knowledge about the activity of such organisations."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, let us look at one exhibit of the Prosecution together, that relates to the cooperation between political parties and charity institutions of the Muslim organisations, P 01794. You have it in the pink binder and you can either find it there or you can see it on the screen. It's the first document in the bundle, and we already have it in e-court. This is in fact a document signed by representatives of the Muslim institutions of Capljina, the Party of Democratic Action, SDA, the Islamic community, the cultural society of Muslims called revival, Preporod, representatives of Merhamet, and the Muslim youth association held on the 2nd of April in Capljina, 2nd of April 1993. Do you know the people who signed this, SDA Capljina, Satko Bitanga, do you know this man?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Islamic community, Nazif Basic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And below that, we see the words, "Main imam," and it says, Hasim Efendi Palic. It's not quite legible. Did I pronounce it well, Hasan Efendi Palic, chief imam. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know this man?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was my colleague in Capljina. Unfortunately he's no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On behalf of Merhamet, Mr. Alija Suta and I can't see the name of the second person, I think it is Admir Mace is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And on behalf of Preporod, revival, Senad Hasanagic?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at this. Some political issues very topical at the time, were mentioned in this document, points 1 and 2, we can comments on the others as well but these two are purely political. It says in para 1, "Support is hereby given to the Vance-Owen plan, signed by the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, and the president of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mate Boban, as well as the previously signed Muslim-Croatian agreement, and we demand urgent implementation of the signed documents at all levels and wherever possible." Para 2 reads, "We hereby call on all patriotic forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to do everything possible for peace to be restored to this destroyed, scattered, and assailed by the defiant homeland of ours and that we may jointly defend it and rebuild it according to the wishes of all its citizens." Do you remember this communique and do you remember if you took part in it in any way?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I probably was aware of it then. It must have been topical at the time but I really don't recall it. You don't see my name here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. But you see the names of people from the Islamic community and Merhamet, who collaborated with you at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You spoke in your statement about the repercussions of the events in Donji Vakuf and Prozor, of early 1993, on the relations between Muslims and Croats in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It transpires from your statement that on the 29th of June 1993 on your way back from Split when you were escorting the Merhamet convoy you were stopped in Doljani at the border crossing -- let's make this clear: That's a border crossing between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the fact that on the 30th of June, July, that the BH army together with Muslim soldiers who were in the HVO at the time attacked in Mostar North Camp barracks, took control of it and took control of the area around Leticia, Potoci, Rastane, Bijelo Polje and arrested most of the soldiers of the HVO and Croatian civilians? Did you know about these events at the time? And I'm linking that up to the events when you were coming back from Split. So I assume that it was an event that was well known to you in Capljina too?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about that. I knew about the conflict in Mostar already in Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know that this act was condemned by the SDA of Mostar too?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you about that because from the first document, we can see that there was cooperation between the SDA, the Merhamet, the Islamic community, so did you know that this act was condemned by the SDA of Mostar, the act on the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but it wouldn't surprise me if it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We are going to go through the document together because we have it. It is 2D 00082, 2D 00082, you have it in the binder but you can read it here. Perhaps that's easier. It's just one page. There we have it. Let's establish first whether we know who the signatories are. It says, "for the Party of Democratic Action, Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic." You knew the man? You know him, do you, from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew who this is about but we didn't know each other personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And did you know the president of the Muslim Democratic party of Mostar, Mohamed Alic?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You didn't know him or hear of him?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I don't now either.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, since you say that it wouldn't surprise you if that was done, let's just go through this document. And it says, "considering the current security in Mostar the Executive Committee of the SDA party of Mostar and the Muslim democratic party of Mostar, at a joint extraordinary meeting, emergency meeting, held on the 30th of June 1993 in Mostar, issues the following announcement. Regarding the BH army attack on the HVO units in Mostar, which was announced yesterday on the 29th of June 1993, at the press conference of the 4th Corps ABiH army command uncovers all the dirty political games by which the Muslim people are to be brought inside some new Yugoslavia or Greater Serbia." I'm not going to read it all, just parts of it. It goes on to say that the Muslim people, and their politics on BiH territory will never accept political solutions exacted by force by suffering and loss of life of innocent people among the Muslim and Croatian people. Now, point 2, I'm going to summarise. It says at this moment the SDA of Mostar in cooperation with the leaders of the HZ HB, the HVO Main Staff, HDZ county [as interpreted], and so on, are undertaking concrete action to put an end to the hostilities and create conditions for a normal life, normal communication between the two sides. Now, do you remember during that period and we are talking about the 30th of June that activities of this kind were really underway and that after the conflicts that had taken place before that attempts were made to normalise the situation and bring life back to normal in Mostar and the surrounding areas, which included Capljina, too?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that I never agreed with this person Hadziosmanovic and the SDA, the regional SDA party. I think that they betrayed the interests of my country and my people, and I do not justify or support their actions, and quite obviously the regional SDA led by Dr. Hadziosmanovic had collaborated with the HVO. That's quite obvious. I was convinced of that then and I'm convinced of that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we conclude, then, or can I sum up by saying that among the Muslim -- I'm sorry that I have to keep saying "the Muslim," but you know why I have to use this term? I know that we say Bosniaks now but we are talking about this period of time when people referred to the same people as Muslims. So do you allow for the possibility that all Muslims did not have the same vision as to how the problem should be solved. Quite obviously some people had different views and thought the problem could be solved differently, and I'm talking about those turbulent times. So that's the periods we are focusing on now when this was actually taking place there were people who thought this could be solved in a different way, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if Citluk were to be attacked I would have said the same thing and thought the same thing but do you know where North Camp is? North Camp is in the centre of Mostar so nobody was attacked, all that could be done there was to liberate what was belonged jointly to all the people of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, I agree with you and that's why it shouldn't have been attacked especially not by soldiers who belonged to the HVO and were Muslims and were there. But I really don't want you -- to involve you or myself into a military story, the military aspect. I wish to deal with questions of Caritas and the political influence of Caritas on the life of the people in the area. But I'll go back to my question now and that is, and you didn't give me an answer to it, and it was whether in your opinion during that period of time there really did exist a political consensus or whether certain acts were being undertaken from Zagreb and Sarajevo in order to calm the situation down in the area. Am I right there? Can you remember when this happened?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You are quite right. Of course, efforts were made to lower tensions but we must bear in mind that at that time too, and much before that time and after that time as well, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were-- Bosnia-Herzegovina was a Croatian hostage, so that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say that Bosnia-Herzegovina was Croatia's hostage. I say once again that I didn't wish to speak about politics. But from the aspects of Capljina, you know that I am from Sarajevo, so whose hostage was I at the time? Any way, we can agree to help the Trial Chamber and everybody else throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. On all its territory different things were going on, different conflicts were going on between different ethnic groups and even between the same ethnic groups, too. Do you and I agree on that point?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree. There were people who thought differently, acted differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Within any ethnic -- every ethnic group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's go back to the Merhamet now. Merhamet and its task or assignment was to hand out assistance to the civilian population, that's what it did; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was its principal task.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say it was its principal task. Can we ask whether a charity organisation can provide assistance to the army, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I didn't ever say that. I didn't say that it helped the army but it did help the families of soldiers, those who were in the HVO and BH army because soldiers had families, did they not? So the -- Merhamet assisted their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I just asked you because you said their principal task so I thought, well, what did you have in mind other than citizens?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the priority task of Merhamet, to help the citizens. First of all refugees and then the citizens as well to provide them with the basics for life. That's the basic goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But we agree, you and I, that that known of these clarity institutions could hand out food to the army?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and in principle it didn't need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us take a look together now at another document. Perhaps you know some of these events. Can we look at document 2D 00283 now, please? I think you'll be able to see it better on e-court because the copy is rather bad. 2D 00283 is the document number. It doesn't seem to be that document. It's a document of the 4th Corps command. Let's wait for it a moment to appear on our screens. We need a bit more time but anyway, thank you. I'm not in a panic over time. We can wait, afford to wait. Have you found it in your binder, Witness, perhaps, so that we can start off? It is 2D in my pink binder, 2D 00 -- here we have it. It's come up on our screens now. Any way we see that it says 4th Corps command. The date is rather important and it is the 11th of December 1992 and it says, "information about MTS in the port of Ploce is being sent out by the 4th Corps to the Main Staff of the armed forces of the ABiH." Now, do you recognise some of the events? It says please inform the Merhamet of Sarajevo that in the port of Ploce for already two months clothing and boots for Merhamet Sarajevo have already been stored there. Nobody has taken over these resources and heavy duty has to be paid for the goods remaining in the port. And then it says the above-mentioned information we received from the representative of the Mostar Merhamet. And then it goes on to say if the Sarajevo Merhamet is not able to take over the goods, that it should be done by the Merhamet in Mostar. Now, look at point 2 and that's why I asked you the question in the first place about what the task of Merhamet was. It says up until now we have not received any telefax linked to ensuring food for members of the 4th Corps, and we checked out -- checked this out with the -- Merhamet and they tell us that they didn't receive the shipment either. If it hasn't already been sent, then send a telefax to the Mostar Merhamet and the number is quoted, because the old telefax is -- fax machine is out of order. We can see the signature, BD commander, 4th Corps, A Pasalic. Let me remind you we are talking about the 11th of December 1992. Now, do you know why I'm reminding you of that date? Because I know that in Mostar on the broader region around it, in certain periods of time, there was a greater need for food and that the army had a food supply shortage although I don't suppose that this was the situation at this time. Now from this document, does it emerge that Merhamet of Mostar supplied food to the BH army as well or, rather, the 4th Corps, and did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry at this point, Ms. Nozica, I cannot help being a bit astonished at seeing a document which purports to be a written communication from the commander of an army corps written by hand. I cannot remember having ever seen such a document from that level, at least not in the 20th century. In the 19th, yes, I've seen it. But is there any explanation?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a moment ago when the Prosecution showed a similar document, you saw one written in hand, and it was by a fairly high-ranking officer. That was a problem that was faced in that period of time and we will encounter quite a few similar documents written in hand but I'd like to ask the witness whether he can confirm whether the signatory was indeed the person who occupied that post and whether the witness knows anything about those events. If not, there will be ample opportunity to go through documents of this kind, handwritten ones, at a later date. Unfortunately my country this is not very rare, as you say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave it at that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Arif Pasalic without a doubt was the commander of the 4th Corps. There is nothing doubtful about that. Now, what this is about I really can't say. I wasn't kept abreast.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you never heard about this shipment of clothing that was in Ploce harbour for a long time? I thought you might know something about that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had heard of many worse cases. 180 trucks of the Merhamet had been seized, so as to boots and clothing, that's negligible, if you compare it to this other instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm not seeking about anything seized but he'll come to that I'm going to speak about the reasons for things seizing things but if we go back to point 3 of this document, we are dealing with the technical reasons and shortcomings. It says, we consider that it is indispensable to have representatives of government and the authorities in Ploce harbour so that these errors committed in points 1 should not be repeated. Especially since large quantities of food, fuel and other MTS, materiel and technical equipment, passes through the port. Therefore, it is necessary to keep in constant communication. So we are not talking about seizing anything. We are talking about the fault on somebody's part for not picking up the goods on time. So that's what this document is about and you can confirm that. Now, whether you don't remember this incident, please say so and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just for the record note that this is not a document which is addressed to Merhamet but it is addressed to the secret service. So it's not evidence of direct contact between the army and Merhamet. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I read the heading and I said to whom it was addressed. The 4th Corps sent it to the Main Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let us move on to the last topic and the last document that I have. You have just mentioned, now and before, that some convoys were stopped. You seemed to know a lot about that. You said that you were escorting a convoy yourself on the 29th of June when you were stopped in Doljani. Please, did you know that there was -- there were occurrences of abuse of these aid shipments that Merhamet sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Before this incident where you were involved yourself, do you know that sometimes weapons were transported in Merhamet lorries to Bosnia, together with aid?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that we were stopped in Doljani. I said that we were taken to Dretelj and arrested. Two of my colleagues remained in Dretelj for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you hear of abuses of aid convoys to transport weapons? I know that your colleagues were detained in Dretelj, but you yourself were released immediately. That's why I said you were stopped. Did you hear of instances of abuse? And do you have any knowledge that such things happened?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose, like in any line of work, there was sometimes abuse, but I'm sure that nothing could be transported to Bosnia without the knowledge of Croatian authorities. It was a very porous and transparent border.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at Exhibit? --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This exhibit explains exactly what we've been discussing. 2D 00008. It's a large document and I'll go through this document with you very quickly. This is a special report from the military police administration, the section of general and traffic military police. The date is 23rd February 1993. This document has many attachments. It says, "on the 23rd of February 1993, at the Doljani check-point," that's the same place where you were stopped, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "The following vehicles were stopped. Licence plates of Gorazde," and we have the number, "with a trailer, transporting goods on the waybill number" so and so, "transporting humanitarian aid for Merhamet Gorazde. A detailed search at the military police administration, it was established that the vehicles contained not only humanitarian aid but also military equipment (weapons) specified in the attachment." Since these -- this shipment reached Ljubuski, it's obvious that it did cross the border in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we look at the next page? It's a record of interview conducted on the 25th of February 1993 and this is an interview with one of the drivers who says -- can we scroll down a little? This driver was questioned on the 25th of February and he says, I'll read this, "On the 12th of February," it's the second sentence in the second paragraph, "I reported to Merhamet, Split to Suad Sogolj, brother of Sejo Sogolj." Did you know these two persons named Sogolj?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "Sejo Sogolj, whose vehicle I was driving, the three of us got into the lorry together, went to Zagreb in order to load some humanitarian aid. When we arrived in Zagreb, we reported at Sajmiste warehouse number 23. I didn't go into the warehouse, nor did I watch the goods being loaded. I only heard that the inscription on the shipment indicated that it contained medicines and some sort of humanitarian aid. After that we went to Zitnjak and loaded the rest of the goods. Everything was negotiated by Suad Sogolj, and I did not interfere in anything because I was not interested." The translation of this record of interview was in fact -- contains only the last page of the translation because there was some sort of mistake when it was uploaded into e-court. The document is 2D 03021. Another driver explains gives the same story approximately but he says, "when I arrived in Zagreb, Ajanovic, Zejnil," second page, in Croatian, it's 2D 03003, let the witness see it, if you have -- you have the binder, but we in the courtroom also need to see it. 0003 are the last numbers. The exhibit number is 2D 00008, page 3. Next page, please. There it is. Zejnil Ajanovic is the second driver. Can we scroll down a little? A little lower. There it is. He says, "When I arrived in Zagreb, I immediately reported to Sajmiste, warehouse number 23 where I used to collect humanitarian aid before. I reported to Suad Sogolj and there was Sefko Omerbasic with him as well as Rizvanbegovic. The three of them had prepared this humanitarian aid for Gorazde. You know Mr. Omerbasic don't you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At that time -- he was just assisting Caritas at that time, and he was working mainly with the Islamic community.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was mainly working for the Croatian. He was the chief imam for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Next page, please. Can we go through all the pages one by one? The next page in Croatian is 2 in this attachment. He says, "I transported weapons even earlier but on those occasions I had papers for legal transportation of weapons. This time, however, I did not. I claim that I did not know anything about it. And any explanation about these weapons could only be given by Suad Sogolj, Rizvanbegovic, and Sefko Omerbasic." Document 30177 contains a description of these weapons. If we look at the next page of this document, and can we move on immediately to the next page, to see the list of weapons? It's an impressive list. We will go through it together. OSA two pieces, military sniper, three pieces, under 6 we see semi-automatic rifle, PM. Isn't that semi-automatic rifle? Four pieces. The witness is probably seeing this in e-court. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] PM is not a semi-automatic rifle. It's a light machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. I will no longer try to decipher any abbreviations to avoid showing my ignorance again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Number 12, next page. Under number 12, we see an RPG, we see how many pieces. Under number 3, Zolja hand-held rocket-launcher, six pieces -- sorry, 16, then we have RPG shells, instantaneous RPG shells on the next page we see PAP, although I know what it means, I won't say it. It says 19 pieces. It's a semi-automatic rifle this time. On the next page, it contains -- we see another list. Can we just go through this list very, very quickly and go to photographs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I wonder whether in view of a certain tightness of time this is necessary because the witness is not an expert on weapons, as far as I can tell, and he has not said that he has any knowledge of this particular transport.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it is rather important to discuss this with the witness who was a member of Merhamet and who a personal experience of arrest, as he put it, and I'll accept his term, because of the goods he was transporting. I think it is important to establish that such incidents happened, that weapons were indeed transported together with humanitarian goods. I am sorry if this is taking time. I'm going to finish as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I fully accept that, absolutely. The question is whether one has to go into details and count the grenades. One sees in the pictures there is a lot of them. Isn't that enough?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm doing this for your benefit because you frequently insist on details. You have the pictures in front of you but the witness doesn't and the rest of the courtroom doesn't. That's why I really wanted to move on to the pictures, as far as -- as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't know what the problem is, why we are moving through the document so slowly. Can you go to -- move on to the pictures in your binder and next page then, please go on through the document further on. There it is. Can you please put this in e-court, these photographs, so that we see what I am saying? If we can see another two photographs and I won't insist any further, yes, and one more, please. So we see all that is in this list of weapons and my final question, which you have already answered in part, such things were possible and they did happen, but you were aware of them. Would you be notified if something like this happened.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really know, because I went out to collect supplies of humanitarian aid only two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I didn't mean you personally and physically, but did Merhamet as an organisation have some sort of central head office? Would you be notified of such incidents?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you with full responsibility that we never received a gram of flour from the Sarajevo Merhamet. We received more from Caritas. And even if I had been the -- at the very top of Merhamet, I wouldn't have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you were doing the job of Merhamet in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. My job was to be the imam, and I very occasionally got involved in picking up supplies or procuring something from Merhamet or Caritas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I wanted to show precisely this: That stopping these convoys was justified because of these incidents.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are saying that we were arrested because of commodities. Can anybody be arrested because of flour? I know exactly why I was arrested. It was not because of the commodities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that it makes sense to stop convoys at the border and to search the convoys.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in our case, the goods were not searched and they were not inspected before we were arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My colleague tells me that you testified yesterday that you were a member -- just a minute. On page 18 of yesterday's record, you said that you were a member of that body and that you were involved in procurement.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's precisely the reason why I asked you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A brief question from me, Witness.
