On the basis of the photographs, we see that this charity organisation, and I'm going to use the conditional tense here, allegedly carried arms. Now, with respect to your administrative function in the Merhamet, can you give us an explanation for that, how that came about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think that could have happened at all without the knowledge of the Croatian authorities. Sometimes they would let through some goods, and then they would stop it and then they would stop them and take them over. So things like that happened. But not convoys and trucks of the Merhamet, but probably some other truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see photographs of trucks there. We have the numbers of the licence plates too. Now, these trucks were borrowed by Merhamet, lent out by them, or were they -- what were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that the Merhamet didn't have its own trucks. So for its services, it had to procure some trucks. It didn't have its own trucks, at least I didn't know of any trucks that it had in its possession, that it possessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there were humanitarian convoys, Caritas, Merhamet or any other charity organisation, wasn't it the practice to place inscriptions up on the trucks carrying the goods which would say, Caritas or Merhamet or whatever, or was that done without any markings, any reference, to the organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did have some readily recognisable markings so that people knew which organisation and institution was involved. So they were marked. Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, judging by the photographs, were there inscriptions on these trucks or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, obviously it was a truck with a Gorazde registration plate and Gorazde was under siege for a few years. It was under an encirclement. So most probably people fought or tried to come by weapons in various ways. Otherwise they couldn't have survived. Although in principle, of course, I don't justify meddling-- Merhamet's meddling and involvement in things like that, if it did do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, as a religious man with a responsible post and member of the Merhamet, together with the other responsible individuals, did you raise this type of problem? Did you discuss it, that could throw a dark shadow over humanitarian activities? And if you did discuss such issues, what measures did you take to prevent this type of thing happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't talk to anybody, nor was I kept abreast of anything like this going on. I didn't have the need to be involved in anything like that because where I was people were in the HVO ultimately. They were armed. So I didn't have to deal with any issues of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Next Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Praljak has a few questions about the events that took place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: To start off with, let me ask you this: While you were in Gabela, was it more difficult for you to suffer impingements of your dignity or the fact that you were in prison and you had to contend with the hardships that prevailed under those conditions?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally found it more difficult to feel that I had been degraded and suffer degradation because I myself wasn't physically abused, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is this, then: I hope you'll understand that I'm going to ask you some broader questions about what went on in 1992 and 1993, and that my questions do not want to minimise what happened to you, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. You can ask me whatever you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, it's always difficult for me to fully prepare for my questions if we don't have a pause. Let's clarify the arrival of Brigadier Dzanko down there, and the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, asked you, and you confirmed that, that Dzanko emphasised that he had come there on a private visit; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But we did not clarify the question of what he was saying when he said he came to visit some soldiers who were with him, who had been with him. Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't say that. Obviously he had come to visit the camp and the detainees but among those detainees there were some of his former soldiers. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, do you know that at the beginning of the aggression against Croatia in 1991, there were a lot of Bosniak Muslims, I'm going to use both terms, Bosniaks and Muslims, because we are referring to that period of time, that many of them voluntarily came to enlist in the Croatian army? Do you know that? To join up.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know many of them who fought as volunteers on the Croatian side [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that they had residence in Bosnia-Herzegovina and were over there either doing labour work, kingon [phoen] construction sites, ship-building yards or whatever?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that brigadier Dzanko led operations in the south of Dubrovnik or to the south of Dubrovnik, Slano, or for instance --

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that. I'm not aware of that. But I assumed he was somewhere on the southern battle front any way, that he engaged in fighting on the southern front somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a very slight intervention. On page 50, line 1, the witness said that he knew that Bosniak Muslims voluntarily fought on the Croatian side. That is what it says on the transcript. It says in the Croatian army. The HV. The witness said in Croatia, in Croatia. Perhaps you could repeat that, Witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You meant the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In the Croatian army, you mean?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: With good reason, can we assume that Dzanko, Brigadier Dzanko, asked about those soldiers, the ones who were in the Croatian army, and then crossed over later on, after the conflict ceased in Croatia, and there was a truce, that they moved to the HVO and to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even think about that. It wasn't vital, as far as I was concerned. He just mentioned it in passing. It was quite clear to me why he was there. Now, this didn't trouble me where the soldiers were or even who they were. I wasn't interested in that at all at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the soldiers who were in the Croatian army and were originally from Bosnia-Herzegovina, both Croats and Muslim Bosniaks, after the truce at the beginning of 1992 in Croatia, in large numbers returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina and joined the HVO units and the BH army when Bosnia and Herzegovina was attacked?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. We've clarified that point now about Dzanko. I'd like you now just quickly to look at 1992. In the spring, the JNA arrived in Stolac and the Dubrave plateau; is that correct? 1992, the spring of 1992 I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that is correct. They arrived in the autumn, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then the reservists from Montenegro arrived?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was roughly what it was like.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it also correct that when they entered the Dubrave plateau, those units, that the Croatian Defence Council put up some sort of resistance?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a joint resistance was put up by the Bosniaks, the Bosniaks put up resistance, and they were not part of the HVO at the time. If you're talking about the events at Domanovici, when the JNA attacked Mostar and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is it correct that after the arrival of these reservists, the Croats moved out of the area, they fled?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know about that. Some did, some did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But most of them did. Did the majority leave?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you could put it that way. We could say that they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would it also be correct to say that when the reservists started drinking and shooting around in 1992, the spring of 1992, around Stolac and Dubrave plateau, that between 12.000 and 15.000 Muslims left that area and went either to Dalmatia, Western Herzegovina or wherever. Any way, across the river Neretva and Bregava down there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct but I'm not sure of the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Is it also correct that at the time, you also went to the island of Brac to join your family?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No my family did but I left 40 days later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Now, at the time, you and the members of your family or anybody else whom you happened to talk to of your parishioners tell you that they had any kind of negative emotional or structural attitude towards Muslims in the area?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have to wait for anybody to tell me that. I was convinced of that, and that's how I experienced it, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So they took you in with an open heart. Can we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And with a pure spirit?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, from other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the Serbian aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, already at that time in Croatia, was -- were there hundreds of thousands of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims and Croats alike, of course?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there was a very large number. I know that on one particular day, some people arrived, 5.000 of them, in one day, and they had been held up at Ilidza. So yes, that was correct. And I was in Split at the time, let me just tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it also correct that Croatia, who was -- a third of which was occupied and at all intents and purposes destroyed, the electricity system, its companies, and so on, found accommodation for those refugees in all the available hotels and facilities, holiday homes, camps that it had at its disposal, in private houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the best possible accommodation under the circumstances was provided to these people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, with respect to feeding the population, humanitarian organisations later joined in and the UNHCR. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody had to pay for electricity or water or garbage disposal or any other utilities and things that somebody has to pay for in a country? Did anybody have to pay for services of that kind in Croatia, do you know about that, any of these people who came in?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some humanitarian organisations, Arabic ones to begin with, did pay some rent to certain families but I think that was negligible if we look at the collective accommodation and the -- for the vast majority of the expelled and displaced population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know of a single case where somebody, a Bosniak Muslim, who was a refugee or displaced person from Bosnia-Herzegovina, at any time had to pay for any medical care and attention that he might need -- have needed in Split, Zagreb, Rijeka, Pula, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I myself was in good health so I didn't have to ask for any medical aid but I don't think there were any difficulties in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'd like now to go back for a moment, if I may, to the word "collaboration" that you used, that the SDA had with the HVO and I'd like to ask you the following: Do you know that the president, or, rather, member of the Executive Board of the SDA of Stolac, Mr. Alija Rizvanbegovic, was excluded from the SDA because he was accused of not working hard enough, especially to organise the Muslims militarily before the Chetniks entered Stolac where he refused any cooperation with the Croats, who insisted on the joint defence -- a joint defence for Stolac before the Chetniks entered, later on created, set up his own authority in Stolac, with the Serbs? Are you aware of that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that something was going on. Now, what form that authority and governance took, I don't know. In my view, he played a very negative role at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that even before the war, and during the war, it is truth that is killed fastest by everyone?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the truth dies last.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You mean hope dies last?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, hope and truth, let me tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were you even then able to follow the dissatisfaction rising among some Croats over the collaboration of Mr. Rizvanbegovic with the Croats in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything about the developments in Stolac because I had no contact with them. I don't think I even travelled there at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then you probably don't know --

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what happened when the JNA arrived and, of course, I don't approve of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You don't know that that gentleman organised the setting up of barricades when the HVO, together with some Muslims who had prepared to defend Stolac, organised the defence of the town?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I wasn't there. I couldn't really comment on that. It's possible, in view of all that happened in Stolac, that is a possibility, but I really can't comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that this same gentleman later became the main ideologist of the Bregava Brigade comprised exclusively of Bosniak men, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a possibility but, you know, I don't even know that man. I really don't know him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. All right. It's a very simple answer. You don't know and that's it. The indictment here starts with the so-called agreement on the division of Bosnia between the Croatian president, Franjo Tudjman, and Slobodan Milosevic. Was it simple, within the framework of that alleged agreement, for all Bosniak Muslim refugees, in Croatia, to be sent to the western borders with Hungary, Austria and Italy, and to be told, we have no room for you. We have a war on our hands. Europe is free; they don't have a war there. Would that have been logical?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the plan was. All I know was that Muslims did go to third countries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: According to the information that you have, is it the case that over a million and a half people were displaced from Bosnia and Herzegovina in different ways?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that Croatia was simply unable to admit 1 million and a half but it did admit 250.000 to 300.000 people, and many others passed through on their way to third countries?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Wouldn't it have been logical, in the June of 1993, to simply prohibit entry to all Bosniaks, all Muslims, who had fled from the Dubrave plateau, to burn all the mosques, and to implement that alleged agreement between Karadzic and Boban, made in Graz?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well in my eyes, it's into the an alleged agreement because I heard the participants say on TV that that agreement was reached and what the agreement was concerning Neretva and the left bank of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, then, can you explain to me why I, Petkovic [as interpreted], led an attack across the Neretva when the Neretva was the border both in Mostar and here, because we were renegades from the accepted policy or because it was our own initiative? How would you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an explanation. I think the areas of interest were already divided. It was already well established what should be under the control of the HVO and what was to be under the control of the Serbs. We, the Bosniaks, had no place there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, I can accept that it is your opinion, but we have to follow some sort of logic. If an agreement was signed saying that the Neretva is the border, then why would I be leading an attack in Mostar targeting the other bank? Why would Croats and Muslims both have to lay down their lives? Why would Croats and Muslims, if it had been agreed that Stolac belongs to the Serbs, all go back if there is an agreement that this is an ethnic Croatian area? The logic fails us. Where does it fail us here?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that -- I know that two Bosniaks got killed. I know that none of the Serbs were killed. I don't know about the Croats. I know that the agreement was already reached then. I know that the spheres of interests had been divided.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. We heard a document read out here saying that only a Bivolje Brdo, Bivolje hill, three persons were killed but I'm not going to go into that with you. Do you know that the port of Ploce at the time when humanitarian aid was going to Bosnia-Herzegovina, shipped over 700.000 tonnes of commodities to Bosnia and Herzegovina, including to the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that. I know even the person at the port who dispatched that, who was in charge of this. His name was Martin Ragus.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So it was 700.000 tonnes and that is equivalent to 70.000 lorries with a capacity of 10.000 tonnes.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: There were certain problems with certain convoys, but 70.000 lorries passed. Do you know that it was only with under 5 per cent of lorries that there were any problems?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that the only convoys that were safe were those organised by the UNHCR. All the others were not safe. In some places in western Herzegovina, incidents happened where they would unload goods from 180 trucks in one go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You know about that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the Tuzla convoy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We have discussed the Tuzla convoy many times in this courtroom, and the Trial Chamber knows that 90 per cent of that convoy did pass through, although with difficulty. My question is this: Is it the case that everything that was good was not the subject of discussion but the few scary stories circulate add great deal and were given a great deal of publicity. Isn't that the psychology of war?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you are talking about this practice to stop Merhamet convoys as if it were something unusual, an individual incident, but it was just normal practice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you underload 700.000 tonnes in just one port in Croatia or in four ports in Croatia, 700.000 tonnes of humanitarian aid, and that is equivalent to 70.000 lorries carrying 10.000 tonnes each, I did the calculation, only under 5 per cent of those lorries ever encountered any problems. Let us change tack. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in end 1992 or maybe early 1993, as we heard from the chief of the Main Staff of ABiH, General Sefer Halilovic, numbered 220.000 men -- sorry, no, General Petkovic corrects me, 261.500 men. Do you know of this number and do you know of this statement by General Halilovic, that was the strength of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have had the men but they were not a force because they did not have enough weapons due to the embargo from both sides. They were simply not armed. They had the numbers, maybe, but not the strength, not the force.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Never mind. We'll leave that to military experts. But do you know that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had tanks, helicopters, howitzers, mortars, that de facto the greatest number of these men had rifles, semi-automatic rifles, otherwise how would they have put up resistance?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did have some of those things, but compared to the forces they were fighting, it was negligible. It was nil.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you imagine any channel for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to get its military supplies except through Croatia, with the knowledge of Croatia, and with the help of Croatia, with the help of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO? Do you know of any other channel?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the arms shipments came through Croatia. It was the most available, the most open one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, if it was the most open, then there were other channels that were open. Which would you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, things could also be bought from Serbs, at least that's what I heard, although for a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it the truth that these convoys also carried fuel and oil for the requirements of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, without any delay, without any hindrance?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Some quantities possibly did pass.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. I would now like to go back to the beginning of democratic changes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it correct that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was imprisoned twice in Tito's Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know he was arrested twice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it the case that under that communist regime he fought for the rights of what was then the still unrecognised Muslim nation, Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He fought for democracy and human rights.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that while in prison, as a political thinker, he wrote a document titled, "The Islamic Declaration."

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that on the eve of the first parliamentary elections, when Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was already the leader of the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, his book was printed with a circulation of 200, 250.000 copies and distributed among the members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I had that book but I bought it myself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it the case that this book, "the Islamic Declaration," by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, envisages struggle for a civic state until Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina form 50 per cent of the population, whereupon an Islamic state would be instituted? Was that the political platform?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina who could call himself an academic or a scientist and who thought that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm asking you something else. Does the book say what I just quoted? Is that written in the book, explicitly in our language, or do you not remember?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's been quite a while since I read the book but I know that that sort of thinking was not the thinking of Alija Izetbegovic. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look, when a book, on the eve of very important structural changes for a state, is printed in 250.000 copies and the author of such a book is the leader of the Muslim Bosniak population, isn't that book considered to be a political manifesto in scientific and academic circles?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that -- you said yourself that under the communist regime, Alija Izetbegovic was imprisoned twice. That book could not even have been printed before. That's why it was printed when it was. I know that we had problems, we who reviewed it, I think, Mr. Filipovic was the one who reviewed it. Those were difficult, hard times.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When a book like that is written in prison it is written by a citizen fighting for a certain political idea, would that be right, a citizen, a citizen, and in this case, it was a citizen named Alija Izetbegovic writing, and when it is published, when it is printed, then Mr. Izetbegovic at the same time was the leader of the Bosniak Muslim people; is that correct? Just tell us whether that was the same time that the book came out in 250.000 copies?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it coincides exactly but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the Bosniak Muslims, intellectuals, sociologists, philosophers, political science experts from Islamic community, from different political parties, anybody, did anybody publicly oppose the stands and positions put forward in that book? Do you know of any such case, or that he questioned Mr. Izetbegovic's positions?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that anybody did that and I don't think it was necessary either. I did not see in it what you saw in it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You're an educated man. Do you know that a social -- a sociopolitical climate is made up of many more positions, viewpoints, sentiments, emotions, and so on and so forth, than actual facts, hard facts that can be studied in our rooms with books? Can our nations have perceptions of things that might be wrong but where the emotions are strong, groups, individuals and a whole ethnic group, a whole nation, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that people have certain prejudicial opinions and perceptions and that they can have negative effects on trends but I don't think that you could class Alija Izetbegovic in that category. He did have prejudices, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Regardless of that, do you think that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, as far as they were concerned, when they saw a book of that kind come out with those positions and stands, did they cause negative perceptions to arise and a feeling that they might be jeopardised, they might be in jeopardy in a state of that kind. Whether they thought so rightly or wrongly, but do you allow that those are the sentiments that might prevail?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is possible, if they listened to what other people say about the book. But if they read the book themselves then I'm sure they would draw the proper conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, let's look at it this way: The Koran is a holy book for the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without a doubt, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, does that book address religious, moral and sociopolitical systems in society for those people who believe in that book? That is to say, religious, moral and socio-political organisations and systems, laws or let me express my better the legal and political setup of a country?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Koran is first of all a moral code, a moral code of conduct. It also deals with some legal issues and in a way it regulates the life of the individual and the community. So you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you accept my claim that -- or assertion that I have read the Koran, well-intentioned, and I know its moral fibre? Do you accept that from me as a fact? Do you believe me?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt it for one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: One of the witnesses that was here before you - he was an imam, too; I don't want to mention his name - in 1992, in Capljina, used publicly the word -- or, rather, for Muslims he said the Koran was the constitution and the jihad was the road? I know what in the Koran interpretation jihad means. Now, my question to you is as follows: Tell me, at that time, with all the turbulent times that we experienced, to utter such a very strong word, which 99.99 per cent of the population does not understand, can you imagine what negative repercussions that causes with another ethnic group? Such as the Croats, for example? So that's my first question. Do you know about that? Can you understand that that can be the case and conceive of something like that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I -- may I give my assessment or do you want me to just give a yes or no answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, I know the meaning and sense of what he was saying, so as far as I'm concerned, you don't have to explain it to me. But what I was asking you was this: What would the perceptions be of what was said on people who didn't know what he had in mind? Would it be negative?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can only be negative.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right, it can only be negative. Now, do you also know from that how much energy one must invest in order to suppress those -- that kind of negative reaction amongst your own people, in your own ethnic group, in order to prevent an emotional aggression on the part of individuals? Do you know how much talk, philosophical explanations and energy generally must be invested or needed to be invested at that time in Capljina, I had to do a lot of shouting and everything else, to quell some 20 youths who would like to react in some way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, of course. And individuals have to make their contribution. Individuals and institutions must do their utmost to prevent such outbreaks from taking place and for the right kind of communication to be able to take place between people, individuals and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry to interrupt the cross-examination but, with respect, it's gone on for a long time and the discussion may be interesting but I don't know whether it really advances or whether it is really relevant to the case. It requires a lot of speculation on the part of the witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. It's quite true, Mr. Praljak, you are taking the witness down hypothetical roads, successive cascade of hypotheticals and one might well ask oneself what the usefulness of it all is. And any way it's 5.30, it's time for our break, and we reconvene in 20 minutes' time, at 10 to 6.00, which will give us until 7.00 and then we'll have to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I don't know if Mr. Praljak has any more questions to ask because there are other Defence teams that are waiting to cross-examine. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have been given time from the Defence counsel up until 25 minutes to 7.00, when Ms. Alaburic will continue. So I would like to provide an answer first to Mr. Kruger. I owe him an answer why the presentation of things of this kind are necessary, and -- well, because they are founded in the indictment. The indictment starts with 1991 and it speaks about the structured quality of the opinions and minds of the Croatian leadership with a view to doing everything that it says in the indictment to the Bosniak Muslim population. And in that same indictment, I think it was the third protagonist is, Mr. -- Mr. Kruger, is my name as a third protagonist. Now, secondly the society is made up of political views, cultural views, artistic views, emotions, a "Weltanshauung" generally, and every society, an organised society, a democratic society, at times has to fight anomalies which rise to the surface and we are witnesses of that if we watch the news every day, whether there are rebellions from the black population of America or the French citizens of Islamic origin rising up or whatever. Without an understanding of things like that, the things we are discussing here now, in my profound opinion, we cannot understand the spiral of war, and how it overflows and how retaliation comes about. But the law is there to punish, to punish when the physical laws are not abided by and that is why there are so many people who, for different reasons, do not recognise that the law exists. War leads to changes in social systems. There is aggression, there is serious destruction, social and state organisations no longer exist and therefore it is an ideal breeding ground for bringing rise to more individuals with more energy and groups to become multiplied which in times of that kind, where morale is at a low ebb, act according to only their own laws and their own assessments and evaluations, which most frequently lead to what the witness experienced himself, Mr. Kajmovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I think that was a very good key word what you mentioned, what the witness experienced himself. And that's what he's here to speak about. He is one stone of a wall the Prosecution tries to build. I admire your rhetoric. You have more than a page now in this speech but this is really to let the witness not give opinions of whether he agrees with you or not but to tell us what he actually lived. And I think the Prosecution has opined in saying you go quite, quite far away from that. So may I recall that we have decided that the accused also can ask questions regarding facts where they were personally present and that the very general discourse which we hear, not for the first time, I think, does not help the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, if you wish to be of assistance to the Chamber, and if you wish to put forward your Defence case, then you must focus on the witness who is here and above all, the documents that were presented to the witness and to the witness testimony, because he told us some important things about what went on in Gabela and the responsibility of each instance from the commander upwards, civilian, military and political leaders, and in those -- all those authorities played a role. So that is what we are interested in, in particular. Of course, it's very interesting to hear your voice about the Koran. That's also interesting but the fact is we are in a judicial system in which the Judges are going to have to form an opinion and pronounce themselves on responsibility and accountability. So if you waste your time, you will not be contributing to your own Defence case. That's what we wish to tell you. What you're saying is very interesting but very interesting on an intellectual level. But that's not going to help you or further your case. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have not heard the Prosecutor ask the witness yet from any crime base aspect whether he knows whether Praljak was in such and such a place at such and such a time or someone else, or whether the witness knows I took part in such and such, whether he has any evidence to prove it or whether he heard about this, whether he knew me earlier, whether he knew my work in the area. None of those questions were asked by the Prosecutor. We didn't hear anything like that being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, not by you so far and you've had the floor for a long time. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I can finally ask that question. And I will. Now, regardless of everything, can we put on the ELMO -- for the benefit of Mr. Kajmovic, could you please take this and put it on the ELMO? It was exhibited as Exhibit 3D 00322. I will ask the witness whether he knows anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You heard about the crime in Ahmici, haven't you, on the 16th of March 1993? Sorry, 16th April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know the whole truth about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you please open and show us on the ELMO the first thing, the crime committed against Croats in Doljani, Jablanica municipality, 3D 13-00178. The first yellow page. On the 28th of July 1993, in Doljani, I will never say Bosniaks or Muslims but I will say some people, some units, killed 63 Croats. Do you know anything about that crime? Have you ever heard anything about it?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know enough to form an opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please open Konjic, 3D 13-0181. In Konjic, in the spring of 1993, according to our information, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather it's 4th Corps, mounted an attack and expelled Croats, and there were 85 victims. Do you know about that case in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about all the mass killings in Herzegovina, I think, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you now open 3D 13-0193, that's Bugojno. Next page, please. Next page. Leaf through it. The overall list of those killed is 118. Did you know about this case as well?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About that one and some others, also in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I won't go on. There were 45 killed in Zenica, again in spring 1993, Kiseljak, 35. My question is, and I think that's a question that has to be asked, is it impossible to prevent the repercussions of such events within the body of one nation? Is it impossible to prevent the effect of such events on a nation?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I am horrified over such crimes but I don't see them as justifying other crimes against other people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm not talking about justification or alibis. I make that reservation at the very beginning. There is no justification for a crime, except those that criminals make for themselves.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept that at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The fact that we do not accept justification and we believe there can be no justification means that we should construct a world without any crimes. My question is: Is that possible? How can you stop it? Do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we need to create is an environment where a criminal cannot get the upper hand and an appropriate philosophy of living.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That Konjic man that you told us about, the Konjic man from your story, the sadist who beat people, he does not represent all the people of Konjic. We have one deviant person. How can you stop him? Is that an understandable question that arises in the mind of everyone who ever tried to stop the spiral of war?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doubtlessly somebody was responsible and duty-bound to stop him and others like him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll move on. You must know certain things even as a regular citizen. Was the mosque in Capljina destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not destroyed. It was damaged a bit on the inside.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was the Orthodox Church in Capljina destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was the mosque in Pocitelj destroyed after the Dayton Accords when the armies were at ease, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It wasn't destroyed before my arrest and I can't say anything about Pocitelj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you went and tried to Visevice and were stopped by the police, was that after the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So after the Dayton Accords, after the truce, the atmosphere still reigned wherein you were stopped by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I was. It was the HVO police with dogs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, are you aware of the fact -- I think it will be interesting for the judges to hear this before taking the recess -- that there is a Franciscan church in Capljina, the church of the Franciscan order, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that by a decision of the Holy See and the bishop of Mostar, as the executor of that decision, Mr. Ratko Peric, the Franciscans should have -- were supposed to leave Capljina and other priests of another order were supposed to take their place?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that despite this decision of the Pope, Catholic believers in Capljina walled in the church, surrounded it with barbed wire and defended it with arms? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the door was really walled in. I don't know anything about the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm telling you this because we need to understand the people who lived there, those people who believe in that church, you know that Catholics are good believers, go to church regularly, as far as you know, is that true?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know most of the people are good church-goers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You also know that the decisions of the Holy See are final and not subject to appeal. When Rome speaks, that is final?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know it's something like that although it's not really scripture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And despite that, do you know that the Franciscans are still in Capljina to date and they won't be thrown out?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who is in Capljina. I know there are Franciscans there. I suppose they are in Capljina as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: This little debate had a purpose and the purpose was to show whether it was really possible to exert effective control over the population of Herzegovina who won't even listen to the Pope. Let us now go back to the part where you spoke about schooling in Capljina and you said that a certain number of Muslim students rebelled against the introduction of the Croatian syllabus and language in schools.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The children rebelled against this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, is it true that in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was said that the official language on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was Serbo-Croat or Croatian-Serb until 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbo-Croat language was the official language, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it the case that the education system in Croatia had the capacity to print the necessary textbooks and prepare the syllabi and the programmes for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although the times were hard, print works were active. Some important books were printed even at that time, including in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Books that were printed in a thousand or so copies, but textbooks, did we have at the time a grammar of the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which time you're talking about, but not at the beginning maybe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In 1992, let's say, did you have a grammar of the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there was not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you have a textbook on orthography, etymology, syntaxes, word creation?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but in any case that doesn't mean you have to impose somebody else's language on us. I would rather be illiterate than have something imposed on me, something that I don't want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know the children in Tuzla and Zenica, including Croatian children, had tuition [as interpreted] in Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised. There were things that were taught to them in English or in German as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, at that time in addition to the subjects that are neutral in a way, chemistry, physics, maths, et cetera, in view of the very small differences in syntax, wasn't it reasonable to accept the Croatian language, at least in name, until you get the chance to call your language the way you wanted? Was it an imposition that you couldn't get over?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It meant to us the loss of our identity. Why didn't you leave Serbo-Croat that existed before? I wouldn't have minded. I would have continued to be literate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You say you were prepared to accept Serbo-Croat, with the Serbian component in the first place?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the language I was taught in primary school. I understand it perfectly and even now I don't consider it as a foreign language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At the time when Sarajevo was shelled, at the time when thousands of people were being expelled, when Vukovar and Dubrovnik were in flames, you thought it was better to accept Serbo-Croat than Croatian as a temporary solution?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think. I would never accept Croatian, at any cost.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about newspapers, radio, and television. While there was a repeater at Velez, did you ever feel any coercion from the Croatian side? Were you ever prevented from freely watching television Sarajevo or listening to Radio Sarajevo and reading newspapers from Sarajevo while they were available?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a while, we watched TV Sarajevo, at the beginning it was the JuTel television. Later on it became difficult and even impossible. And, of course, we had to watch what we could receive, and we could receive only Croatian channels, in order to have a minimum of information. Otherwise we would have been incommunicado.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were the Croatian channels received even before the war in your locality?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me about the Croatian television radio and newspapers. Did they provide you with exhaustive information on the crime in Ahmici? Was it covered up or was it given publicity and discussed? How many times did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean television Zagreb, I think they gave it quite enough publicity and they gave it fair coverage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know about Trucina, near Konjic?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of some crimes were committed there but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 16th of April 1993, on the same day when the crime in Ahmici was perpetrated against Muslims, there was another crime committed in Trucina against Croats. Tell me, have you ever heard on Croatian radio, television, or read in newspapers, about the crime in Trucina, and, if you have, how many times compared to coverage of Ahmici at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember what I read. I read a lot at the time in a variety of magazines, although the situation with newspapers was hard. You could get hold of newspapers, but as to what I read where, I really can't remember and tell you now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You spoke about imposition and about not being prepared to accept the Croatian language. Do you know that in 1992, in Croatia, a special classes, additional classes in Bosnian were organised for Muslim children, refugees?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to hear this position that I hold, and I have to tell you that Mr. Kruger and the entire Prosecution often refer to your country as Bosnia instead of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really notice that. As far as I'm concerned, my country is called Bosnia-Herzegovina and I don't want to split it up but I suppose they have become accustomed to that kind of thing because it existed as Bosnia for a long time, for the longest period of time, in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When Herzegovina was a separate area under Herceg Stjepan?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not in favour of separation. Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's what I like to use. That term.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I am, too, but if Bosnia existed as an independent state, did Herzegovina from Herceg Stjepan exist as an independent unit under Austria?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if we can open up this question of Herceg Stjepan and his son who became converted to Islam. Who knows where we would end up if we took that road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Bosnia is part of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right, a geographical concept?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which has its AVNOJ borders. That's where I was born. That's how I understand my country. And that's my country as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We agree but just give me a simple answer to the question. It's a very simple question. Part of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a geographical concept and part of that is called Bosnia, made up of Bosnian Krajina, Semberija, Posavina, Central Bosnia and eastern Bosnia and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it isn't correct, Mr. Praljak. I don't see Bosnia as a geographical concept. I see it as a state, as the country that I was born in and the country I live in. The sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, is Croatia, the state of Croatia, composed of- well, let's take France. France is composed of Normandy, Provence, and so on. It has its geographical concepts. We are not denying the state of France as such we are just saying that there are parts that are called Provence, Normandy and so on. Do we agree there?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No we don't. They are all Frenchmen and women, French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I must really intervene. This has nothing to do with court proceedings. This is a personal litigation between Mr. Praljak and the witness and both have different opinions about something. It does not -- you're not under an obligation to assist the Chamber. That I concede that. But this really contributes nothing, nothing whatsoever to the task of the Chamber and it's really a waste of time. I'm sorry to say so. My last intervention has not brought much fruit, I'm afraid. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, I simply cannot agree because the Bosniaks, the Bosniaks, Bosnia-Herzegovina is composed of two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak, it's not about whether you agree. Judge Prandler wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I really don't like to interrupt you but I listened carefully and with patience as well but after my colleagues here, the Presiding Judge Antonetti and also Judge Trechsel explained why the Chamber is not very much helped by your questions so to say questions quote unquote but I believe it is a kind of lecture, I am of course, as being a Hungarian, I am very much interested in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I know something about it. I also having -- I graduated from history as well and I taught history and history of law. But at the same time I really feel that it doesn't help the Chamber if we are listening to you and your explanations about the language and about the history, which I may have some comments, but it is not the very place where we have to discuss the historical antecedents and problems in that region of the world we have unfortunately we have been witnesses to. And that's why I believe us and believe me that it would be better if you would concentrate on those practical issues which are related to the case here, and then to have the Bench really to go to -- and achieve a consensus most favourable one for you and for all those who are involved in this issue. So I thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, as we are drawing to the end of the year, it is the season of Christmas boxes, presents, gifts. The Chamber invites you, during the holidays and days we have off, to read all the judgements passed by the Tribunal. There are quite a few of them but, as you have enormous working capacity, in reading those judgements you will discover how the Judges work in order to arrive at their conclusions, and if you look at all the decisions and rulings that were made, and judgements made, you will see how history can be integrated into judgements, and maybe when you've done that, you will come to realise that at the level of questions, when you ask your questions, you might think twice and proceed in a different way because as far as we are concerned, it's very simple. At the end of this trial, we are going to have to draw our own conclusions about the facts, whether there was maltreatment in Gabela, et cetera. So we are going to have to determine all those facts, and we are going to determine the chain of responsibility based on witness testimonies, based on orders, documents and so on. So then, as far as you're concerned, we are going to see whether the -- whether what happened in Gabela was any of your responsibility. We are going to have to rule on that ultimately and that is how we work. That is how a Trial Chamber functions. Now, you've taken almost one hour discussing historical matters, language and linguistical problems, Serbo-Croatian, Croato-Serbian, whatever, now I'm telling you, I'm giving you this advice, read the judgements, Blaskic, Kordic, et cetera, Naletelic, and you will see how the Judges work. Mr. Karnavas you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President, thank you, Your Honours. I certainly don't wish to interrupt but perhaps I may be of some assistance. We do appreciate the judicial hint that we just received. I think it's always helpful for the Trial Chamber to guide us when we get carried away. Of course, on those rare occasions as we tend to do. Perhaps Mr. Praljak could identify the topics that he wishes to discuss and get some guidance as to those topics, whether those topics would be relevant in assisting you and then topics that are not relevant, then he can perhaps present in another -- with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add an observation: I fully accept that history has a certain role to play. What I find difficult to accept is that instead of putting a question to the witness and then awaiting his answer and then going to the next question. Take an example with Mr. Karnavas, he puts a question, he says, yes, no, I don't know, I have forgotten, and sometimes Mr. Karnavas puts a question and we know he accepts -- he expects the witness to say yes. The witness says no. Then comes the next question. You, Mr. Praljak, when the witness says no, and you expect yes, you continue with him and try to persuade him. You argue with him. And this is what makes us lose time because we are not here to teach the witness a lesson. We are just picking his memory and that's all. And that I would like you to accept, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I have accepted that. I just asked about the geography of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not challenging the statehood of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We'll come to that in due course on the basis of documents, my own documents and so on. All I wanted to do was to link up a province of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Bosnian language. But we'll skip that. With questions of this kind I just wanted to help us arrive not only at the chain of command, which is quite simple in its structure, but what I wanted to show was, and these questions served that purpose, was what the power of the chain of command was, how powerful it was. Without explanations of this kind we won't be able to do that. Now my last question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Kajmovic, I was down there in the spring of 1992 myself, and after that, but tell me, while I was there, while I was in the area, did you ever hear, that's how we can put it, did you ever hear that I ever said anything or acted in any way in order to produce evil or that by my words and deeds I produced evil?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say anything specific, really I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. We can have that as an answer too. Now, I've read the indictment, Your Honours, of course, and the complexity, the terrible complexity of all this is that we mustn't reduce it to models of extreme simplicity where the truth eludes us. I don't want to argue. I was there. I know the problems on the ground. And not only the structure of the chain of command but how much power the chain of command had or did not have. And through the witness I wish to show how much power existed, how it burgeoned, how it was diminished, how groups started working. Without that I cannot make my contribution to a just judgement. Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Kajmovic. We just didn't understand ourselves -- each other over geography, I think?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: It's not a question, actually, it's just a brief remark that I would like to make following on from what the other judges have already told Mr. Praljak. Of course, it was very interesting to listen to you and I did listen to you very carefully because I want to understand how -- your way of thinking and things generally, and, yes, you evoked history and geography and spoke about society and so on. But it is precisely the link that we are looking for. We wants to establish the link because crimes were committed and, as the Prosecutor sets out in the indictment, crimes were committed, the Gabela prison is mentioned where we had guards and the HVO prison commander was mentioned, and it could have happened, you might have been the commander of that force at some point, so those are the questions that we face. And you have been able to see that through my questions I always try to understand. Now, the debate that you've been holding with the witness is a very interesting one but what is lacking is the link for us to be able to see and understand whether what was being done in the prison, what was happening in the prison, was something that you had certain responsibility for or certain knowledge of or not. So in my opinion, that is the most important point. And not only to speak in general terms of the difficulties that one has if one governs a state or the geographical problems that one encounters. So it would help the Chamber if you could make the link between the indictment and the witnesses that come here to testify instead of entering into very elaborate debates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you've been able to see that the Judges are unanimous on that point, so give it some thought, let it serve as food for thought because what we are telling you is in your own interests and designed to help you because that is what we mean by a fair trial too, to allow the accused to defend themselves, to throw more light on the allegations that have been made by contributing evidence and proof in their defence. Either through the cross-examination or your own documents that you're going to produce in due course and call your own witnesses in due course. Because between now and the end of the trial, the ends of these proceedings, if you keep speaking about the Serbo-Croatian language, about the problems linked to geography, history and so on and so forth, then all the problems that we have to address and provide answers for and rule on ultimately, you won't have helped us and you won't have helped your own interests. So that is what us three judges are trying to make you understand. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. However, 90 per cent of what we spoke about was refugees, humanitarian convoys, and so on and so forth. You can't say that all my questions and everything I said was just stories and not linked to the indictment. And secondly, we learnt today that the deputy of the Boko Previsic was convicted to appeared of 12 years in prison so we should see who ordered him, who issued orders to him and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Perhaps it would be useful to wind up this debate in the following way. I'd like to indicate that my client always reads the indictment and we keep telling him to read the indictment carefully and I have to say that most of the topics raised today, both language, linguistics, history and so on, are derived from the indictment. They are quoted in the introduction to the indictment. For example, the question of language, let me remind you, the Prosecution claims that the Croatian language is being imposed on Bosniak Muslims, for example, and that that was a form of Croatisation, not to go into all the other details. So that is a thesis put forward in the indictment and we have to defend ourselves in that way, by providing arguments. Secondly, history. History is also in the indictment, because the story begins with the alleged many years on of desire on the part of the Croatian people to take a part of Herzegovina, to create a banovina and so on and so forth. And that's what General Praljak wants to look at, the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You will remember Mr. Praljak's earlier comments, I should like to say technical term that is used in the indictment and in colloquial speech when we say the Bosnian Croats. That concept simply does not exist. What we have is the Bosnia and Herzegovinian Croats and the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Muslims at that time, who are today's Bosniaks, and I'm sure the witness will support me when I say that because that is how every member of that nation thinks today. So it is not that Praljak has broached that area without any grounds. We can speak of the methods he has applied. He is not a lawyer of course so Praljak might not be going about it in the right way but all the topics that he has broached are to be found in the indictment. I know what you're saying, Your Honours, too, that you think that that part of the indictment can perhaps be ignored. However, Your Honours, we have seen here, and I won't go into details because I haven't prepared myself for this debate we have seen judgements in this Tribunal in which some of the facts from the introduction part of the indictment were proved to be or shown to be wrong. So we have to defend ourselves against all the words in the indictment, whether it be in the introduction to the indictment or whichever part of the indictment. So that is what I wanted to bring to your attention. So, Your Honours, if I may be allowed having taken the floor already we've save time by doing this now rather than later on, we would like to refer to the 11 statements we need 300 words more over the limit, so can we use more words as we are writing our reply? And -- we need more words to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As far as the 25 minutes that are left to us, I give the floor to Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours,.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon or good evening. You'll have a much easier time with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The authorisation we gave to Mr. Kovacic is not recorded. So the Chamber has granted approval to the defence of Mr. Praljak to exceed the limit set out in the directive in the guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, briefly again about the media, some questions you were asked derived from your answers and could create the impression that the population of the Dubrave plateau could under some circumstances be exposed to other media apart from those from -- which were actually available to you. Tell me, the TV signal was received in the Dubrave plateau from the repeater at Velez?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this repeater destroyed or damaged already in the first attack in the Serb forces? That's how I will call the JNA and the army of Republika Srpska in the area of Stare, in the environs?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, not only in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But that was when the repeater was destroyed. Tell me, was that repeater in the hands of the Serb army throughout that time, the Serb positions in Velez were precisely around the repeater?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think they had full control.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the press? In 1993, what was available? What could reach the Dubrave plateau? What did you receive?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we had any newspapers coming in. I wasn't able to buy them at the news agents in Capljina. I think there were some magazines from --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From Split. Do you remember some newspaper titles, some names of newspapers, some headlines?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the stories were mostly about war events but I couldn't remember a specific topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could newspapers printed in Sarajevo, such as Oslobodjenje or any other newspaper be delivered to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know. They were probably unable to deliver. Oslobodjenje, though, was also printed in Zenica and some other newspapers, too. So yes there were a few possibilities to get some information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for those newspapers to be sold in various population centres, in Dubrave plateau?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not, since there were none.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From what you know, was the HVO, which you said controlled the Dubrave plateau, preventing the delivery of Muslim press, I'll call it Muslim press, meaning newspapers printed in Sarajevo or any other publishing house?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you agree with me that the HVO really did not try to prevent Sarajevo printed press from reaching you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that wasn't done or whether it was done. I don't think actually they were tolerated under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I want this answer very precise. Do you know that the HVO did anything to prevent Muslim press from reaching the area of Dubrave plateau, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of anything specific cases. Maybe they seized occasionally a shipment of newspapers. I don't know anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Kajmovic, when you were talking about your locality and you said there was a barracks housing the command of the Knez Domagoj brigade. You said the population was largely intimidated by their conduct and you said that soldiers wore black uniforms. Now, concerning that fear, I'll ask you this: Were the combat positions facing the Serb army about ten kilometres away from the place where you lived?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us about those positions facing Serb positions. Were they held by the Bregava Brigade and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One part was held by the Bregava Brigade and another part by mainly by Muslims in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It finally entered the record that it was actually Muslims in the HVO ranks. Do you know that in the first quarter of 1993, HVO included about 1500 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number but the very fact that there were two brigades comprised of Muslims testifies to a large number of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were you actually afraid of when the HVO was in your immediate vicinity, when they had so many Muslims in their ranks?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we are at cross-purposes. I wasn't talking about the HVO or the specific prince Domagoj brigade. I was talking about the people who came especially in black uniforms because as you know the regular HVO did not have such uniforms. But these men, and I heard they were Tuta's men, I don't know whether they were or weren't, but that's what people said, that they were stationed in the school building not in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ever hear of HOS?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of them in the context of something good or something bad?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly in a good context, like people who rose against the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were they dressed as a rule in black, in black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecutor raised the issue of 1993, April 1993, and I would like to come back to that period. You said one thing that was particularly curious related to documents shown you by my colleague, Mrs. Nozica and by Mr. Praljak concerning Hadziosmanovic, the regional board of the SDA, and you used the term "collaboration" with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I really believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the word "collaborator" actually means traitor of one's people, the one who collaborates with the enemy?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that you considered the HVO as the enemy of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as they started doing what they were doing, I started viewing them in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To what time do you date this change of heart? When did you start thinking of them as the enemy of the Croatian -- of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC [Resumed]
